extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary critics, and students of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for novels—especially plot, character, contrivance, surprise, endings, and the fantastic/prophetic aspects—aimed at people who write or critique long-form fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty in the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty at which a novelist should never aim, though he fails if he does not achieve it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty should appear as part of a completed plot rather than being forced; it 'ought to look a little surprised' (Botticelli example). The novelist should not set out merely to manufacture 'beauty' in a prima-donna manner; when it comes it must seem incidental and surprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between plot and character
rubrics_metrics.description: There are in the novel two forces: human beings and a bundle of various things not human beings, and it is the novelist’s business to adjust these two forces and conciliate their claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rigidly canalize human happiness and misery into action alone; characters need means of expression other than solely through plot. The novelist must find the proper relation between causal plotting and letting characters function freely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrivances should spring from character
rubrics_metrics.description: "Incident springs out of character, and having occurred it alters that character... They [Meredith's contrivances] are often delightful, sometimes touching, always unexpected."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrivances (devices that move the plot) are good when they organically emerge from the characters and then react upon them. Such contrivances should produce surprise but feel inevitable in retrospect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot ought to cause surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: "This shock, followed by the feeling, 'Oh, that's all right,' is a sign that all is well with the plot: characters, to be real, ought to run smoothly, but a plot ought to cause surprise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful plot gives shocks that transform characters and the reader's perception; examples include the horse‑whipping episode in Beauchamp’s Career. Surprise should feel earned, not arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concealment/mystery (and its risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealment of a character's inner change can create a dramatic surprise (Meredith's Laetitia), but concealment can also damage character integrity (Charlotte Brontë's slip in Villette).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiding a character's mental development can produce an effective plot thrill, yet it risks appearing inconsistent with the character's established voice or moral stance. Employ concealment only when the effect on character credibility is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-planning; allow growth and openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Gide's view: for a book of this type any plan would be unsuitable... 'I am waiting for reality to dictate to me.' 'To pot with the plot, break it up, boil it down.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An alternative to tightly prearranged plotting is to let the work grow, to mix authorial self and experience with material, and to avoid prearrangement that feels false. Breaking the plot and letting unexpected material in can be a deliberate method (Les Faux Monnayeurs example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plot dominion that impoverishes characters
rubrics_metrics.description: When plot emphasizes causality too strongly, characters are required to contribute too much and become 'dry and thin' (critique of Hardy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force characters to serve the plot at the cost of their vitality; over-emphasis on fate/causality can make characters lifeless except for surface humours. Preserve character autonomy where the novelic medium permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weakness of endings / dénouement problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all novels are feeble at the end... the characters go dead while [the novelist] is at work, and our final impression of them is through deadness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of mechanical winding-up (relying on death or marriage). The need to 'finish' often kills the liveliness of characters; authors should look for endings that preserve rather than flatten character vitality and avoid rote logical tying-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should remain consistent and 'run smoothly'
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters, to be real, ought to run smoothly, but a plot ought to cause surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain believable, internally coherent character behaviour; surprises should come from plot incidents that interact with character, not from characters behaving capriciously merely to serve plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in social detail (avoid 'faking' social values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meredith's novels 'the tailors are not tailors, the cricket matches are not cricket...' — a 'chilly fake' of the social scene is a defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray social settings and customs authentically; superficial or conventional 'props' of society undermine the realism and authority of fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy asks an additional adjustment of the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy 'asks us to pay something extra. It compels us to an adjustment... The fantasist says “Here’s something that could not occur. I must ask you first to accept my book as a whole, and secondly to accept certain things in my book.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing fantastical elements, accept that some readers will balk; the work must earn the extra concession by internal consistency and suitability. Decide whether the intended audience will 'pay the extra sixpence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between fantasy and prophecy (mythologies/gods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy and prophecy are alike in having gods, and unlike in the gods they have; fantasy invokes many small gods (fairies, Hermes), prophecy invokes transcendent deities and the prophetic element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate mythic register for your novel: petty/medieval, mischievous myth (fantasy) or grand, transcendent myth (prophecy). The choice shapes tone, devices, and reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized devices of the fantastic
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices include the introduction of a god/ghost/angel/monster/midget/witch into ordinary life; introducing ordinary men into no‑man's land (future/past/other realms); dividings of personality; parody or adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices are limited in number but can be recombined and renewed; use them knowing their conventional nature and work to make them feel fresh and integral to the book's 'beam of light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth in life vs truth in art; mixing author and material
rubrics_metrics.description: Gide's thesis: truth in life and truth in a novel are not identical; he proposed writers should 'mix themselves up in their material and be rolled over and over by it' rather than subduing reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider strategies that combine autobiographical, factual, and fictional truths. Mixing authorial presence and material can be a method to capture complex truth, but risks lucidity/clarity trade-offs and possible reader boredom if mishandled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical/course construction: have an idea running through the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A course of lectures... must have an idea running through it: a subject and an idea that run through the subject too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For pedagogical or critical presentation, maintain an organizing idea that threads examples and arguments together; otherwise the subject may 'steal off' and critical discourse will drift from the texts under consideration.
